title: Performance trade-offs between single-task and multi-task in multi-source prediction of yield and grain protein content in winter wheat
abstract: Early-season prediction of winter wheat yield and grain protein content is essential for guiding fertilizer and irrigation decisions and reducing uncertainty in variable agroecosystems, as yield affects profitability and quality affects market value and nutrition. Although multi-source data and both single-task learning (STL) and multi-task learning (MTL) are widely used for predicting grain yield and quality, the conditions under which each approach performs best remain poorly understood, especially when data availability, noise, and measurement or computational constraints vary. To address this gap, we conducted a three-year field experiment in Henan Province, China, compiling environmental, agronomic, and proximal-sensing variables across five growth stages. Seven subsets were constructed, including environmental, agronomic, sensor, and combined subsets, and STL/MTL variants of Multilayer Perceptron (MLP), Transformer, and Random Forest (RF) were benchmarked. SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) analysis quantified feature- and stage-level contributions and guided construction of compact Top-K subsets for accuracy–efficiency trade-offs. Multi-source fusion substantially improved accuracy over single-source inputs, with the combined agronomic-sensor subset providing the best performance (yield R 2 = 0.823; GPC R 2 = 0.743). Under the current stage-aggregated multi-source representation, MLPs outperformed Transformers and RFs across configurations, indicating that compact nonlinear models were better suited to the present medium-dimensional tabular setting. MTL provided the greatest benefit with sparse feature sets or imbalanced predictive difficulty, whereas STL performed better when information was abundant and signals were strong. SHAP analysis showed that agronomic and sensor features associated with biomass accumulation, nitrogen status, water availability, and canopy light interception were key drivers of model predictions, particularly during erecting and early grain filling. These findings further show that the value of STL versus MTL depends on data-source composition and information richness, and that SHAP can be used not only for interpretation but also for reduced-feature subset design. Within the present plot-scale setting, this study therefore provides a decision-oriented framework for identifying both accuracy-oriented and efficiency-oriented configurations, with efficiency referring to feature parsimony, reduced input and preprocessing burden, and computational time for winter wheat yield and GPC.

title: Physics-informed deep learning for robust maize leaf area index estimation using multi-source data
Lightweight real-time detection of sweet potato virus disease by a hybrid CNN–Transformer network
abstract: Timely and precise detection of sweet potato virus disease (SPVD) is essential for ensuring crop health and improving yield quality in precision agriculture. However, conventional deep learning models often struggle to capture subtle lesion features under complex field conditions. This paper proposes Swin-SPVDNet, a hybrid CNN-Transformer detection framework with task-specific architectural enhancements that combines convolutional neural networks (CNNs) with a modified Swin Transformer to effectively integrate local spatial details and global contextual information. Unlike conventional hybrid models that simply stack convolutional and transformer blocks, the proposed network introduces three key structural designs: (1) A C2PSA-enhanced convolutional backbone for improved local feature sensitivity. (2) A C3STR module that tightly integrates convolutional operations with Swin Transformer blocks for joint local–global feature interaction. (3) A Residual Attention Block (RAB) that refines feature representations while stabilizing gradient propagation. A field-collected SPVD image dataset was constructed using handheld RGB imaging under real agricultural conditions. Extensive experiments and ablation studies demonstrate that Swin-SPVDNet achieves competitive performance compared with representative state-of-the-art detectors while providing a favorable balance between detection accuracy and deployment efficiency, attaining a mean Average Precision (mAP@0.5) of 86.8%, a precision of 85.1%, and a recall of 75.6%. Compared to Yolov5-v11 models, our approach demonstrates improved robustness in detecting small and irregular lesions, particularly under occlusion and lighting variability. These results confirm the practical value of Swin-SPVDNet for real-time field deployment and support its application in intelligent disease monitoring.

title: Adapting SAM3 for 3D fruit counting with cross-view contrastive learning and Hough voting
abstract: Fruit detection and 3D localization have been shown to be critical for precision agriculture applications, such as yield estimation and robot harvesting tasks. However, real-world agricultural settings can be associated with high density of fruits, strong occlusions, and variable illumination, leading to difficulty in accurately detecting and localizing fruits. Although there exist 2D approaches dedicated for fruit counting, these approaches may easily merge adjacent fruits due to projection effects in dense occlusions, thus limiting their effectiveness. Motivated by this, in this paper, we explore the problem of 3D fruit detection and localization with vision foundation model adaptation and 3D Gaussian-based scene representation. Particularly, we use low-rank adaptation to leverage SAM3 to generate high-quality instance masks with different crops and illuminations. Meanwhile, to address noisy pseudo label issue, we adopt cross-view contrastive learning with uncertainty weighting for enhanced 3D feature representation. Moreover, we devise a Hough voting procedure in the 3D Gaussian space to integrate multi-view evidence of occluded fruits, followed by clustering to estimate the number of fruits as well as their 3D locations. The proposed approach has been extensively tested with thousands of fruits from synthetic orchard scenes, real apple orchard datasets, as well as greenhouse sweet pepper scenes. Experiment results show significant performance gains for densely occluded cases, with the F1-scores reaching 0.971 and 0.977 for plum and mango, respectively. Meanwhile, our approach can achieve more than a twofold boost for 3D instance segmentation over FruitNeRF. More notably, the adapted weights and the post-processing settings transfer from the open-field apple orchard to greenhouse sweet pepper scenes, where only the SAM3 text prompt is changed and the 3D Gaussian representation is still optimized for each new scene.

StomataSeg: Semi-supervised instance segmentation for sorghum stomatal components
abstract: Sorghum is a globally important cereal grown widely in water-limited and stress-prone regions. Its strong drought tolerance makes it a priority crop for climate-resilient agriculture. Improving water-use efficiency in sorghum requires precise characterization of stomatal traits, as stomata control of gas exchange, transpiration and photosynthesis have a major influence on crop performance. Automated analysis of sorghum stomata is difficult because the stomata are small (often less than 40 μ m in length in grasses such as sorghum) and vary in shape across genotypes and leaf surfaces. Automated segmentation contributes to high-throughput stomatal phenotyping, yet current methods still face challenges related to nested small structures and annotation bottlenecks. In this paper, we propose a unified semi-supervised instance segmentation framework for multi-class segmentation of three nested sorghum stomatal components. We collect and annotate a sorghum leaf imagery dataset containing 11,060 human-annotated patches, covering the three stomatal components (pore, guard cell and complex area) across multiple genotypes and leaf surfaces. To improve the detection of tiny structures, we split high-resolution microscopy images into overlapping small patches. We then apply a pseudo-labelling strategy with class-specific confidence filtering and expert verification to unannotated images, producing an additional 56,428 pseudo-labelled patches. Patch-based preprocessing increases the top semantic segmentation mIoU from 65.93% to 70.35% and the top instance segmentation AP from 28.30% to 46.10%. Subsequent pseudo-label retraining further increases overall AP from 46.10% to 49.20% for Mask R-CNN with ConvNeXt-V2. These results demonstrate that combining patch-based preprocessing with semi-supervised learning significantly improves the segmentation of fine stomatal structures. The proposed framework supports scalable extraction of stomatal traits and facilitates broader adoption of AI-driven phenotyping in crop science.

title: Improved point cloud segmentation algorithms for in situ individual plant phenotyping and weight prediction of Chinese cabbage plants using UAV imagery
abstract: With the advancement of precision agriculture and modern breeding techniques, large-scale, efficient, and in situ acquisition of plant phenotypic data has become a critical challenge in research. Traditional manual measurement methods are inefficient and struggle to meet the demand for high-throughput phenotypic data in modern breeding. Consequently, this study proposes a method based on low-altitude drones and three-dimensional (3D) point cloud analysis to achieve in situ, nondestructive phenotypic extraction and weight prediction for individual Chinese cabbage plants. First, RGB images are captured in the field using unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs). Large-scale 3D point clouds are reconstructed through structure from motion with multiview stereo technology. Subsequently, an enhanced graph convolutional neural network (AW-GNN) is proposed, integrating wavelet convolution, adaptive graph structure learning, and attention mechanisms to improve the accuracy and robustness of point cloud semantic segmentation. Building on this foundation, a morphology-guided watershed clustering algorithm is introduced. High-density segmentation of individual plants can be achieved in crowded environments by integrating two-dimensional canopy height maps with 3D point cloud spatial information. Based on the segmentation results, 3D phenotypic parameters, such as plant height, canopy width, and volume, are extracted. Individual plant weight prediction models are constructed using machine learning methods, including support vector regression (SVR) and random forest. Experimental results demonstrate that AW-GNN achieves an Intersection over Union (IoU) of 91.63% in point cloud semantic segmentation, significantly outperforming existing mainstream models. Morphological watershed clustering effectively mitigates undersegmentation and oversegmentation problems encountered by traditional methods under dense plant conditions. For individual plant weight prediction, the SVR model delivers optimal performance with a validation set R 2 of 0.8691 and root mean square error of 0.2810 kg. This study demonstrates the feasibility of achieving individual plant phenotyping and weight prediction in large-scale in situ scenarios using a UAV platform and improved point cloud segmentation algorithms, thereby providing an effective technical approach for high-throughput plant phenotyping analysis and digital breeding decision-making.

title: A physics-informed, behavior-aware digital twin for robust multimodal forecasting of core body temperature in precision livestock farming
abstract: Precision livestock farming requires accurate and timely heat stress prediction to ensure animal welfare and optimize farm management. This study presents a physics-informed digital twin (DT) framework combined with an uncertainty-aware, expert-weighted stacked ensemble for multimodal forecasting of Core Body Temperature (CBT) in dairy cattle. Using the high-frequency, heterogeneous MmCows dataset, the DT integrates an ordinary differential equation (ODE)-based thermoregulation model that simulates metabolic heat production and dissipation, a Gaussian process for capturing cow-specific deviations, a Kalman filter for aligning predictions with real-time sensor data, and a behavioral Markov chain that models activity-state transitions under varying environmental conditions. The DT outputs key physiological indicators, such as predicted CBT, heat stress probability, and behavioral state distributions are fused with raw sensor data and enriched through multi-scale temporal analysis and cross-modal feature engineering to form a comprehensive feature set. The predictive methodology is designed in a three-stage stacked ensemble, where stage 1 trains modality-specific LightGBM ‘expert’ models on distinct feature groups, stage 2 collects their predictions as meta-features, and at stage 3 Optuna-tuned LightGBM meta-model yields the final CBT forecast. Predictive uncertainty is quantified via bootstrapping and validated using Prediction Interval Coverage Probability (PICP). Ablation analysis confirms that incorporating DT-derived features and multimodal fusion substantially enhances performance. The proposed framework achieves a cross-validated R 2 of 0.783, F1 score of 84.25% and PICP of 92.38% for 2-hour ahead forecasting, providing a robust, uncertainty-aware, and physically principled system for early heat stress detection and precision livestock management.

title: Improving greenhouse fruit-production control by integrating reinforcement learning into short-horizon model predictive control
abstract: Greenhouse fruit-production control aims to maximize the economic performance (fruit revenue minus operating costs) while operating within system constraints under external weather disturbances. Control methods need to balance the delayed economic benefit of fruit yield with current operating costs. For such problems, model predictive control (MPC) can handle constraints under future weather disturbances, but can become computationally demanding when using sufficiently long prediction horizons for (relatively large) nonlinear greenhouse fruit production models. In contrast, reinforcement learning (RL) can learn control policies before deployment while considering economic performance beyond MPC’s prediction horizon. However, desired indoor climate ranges are typically incorporated through penalty terms, and performance may degrade under unseen weather trajectories. This work proposes trajectory-selection RL–MPC , a framework that incorporates the economic benefit of fruit yield beyond the MPC prediction horizon into a finite-horizon optimization problem with a relatively short horizon (one hour). The framework uses an RL rollout trajectory to define a terminal region constraint and terminal cost. Next, a nonlinear MPC solves a short-horizon optimization problem with these terminal ingredients to find a local optimum. Finally, the framework selects and executes the first input from the trajectory with the better objective value, either from the MPC-predicted or the RL rollout trajectory. The method is applied to GreenLight, a large-scale nonlinear greenhouse tomato production model that exhibits stiff dynamics. The simulation results show that trajectory-selection RL–MPC with a one-hour prediction horizon matches the closed-loop performance of a high-performing guiding policy while improving over standalone MPC with the same horizon. On 25 weather trajectories held out during policy training, trajectory-selection RL–MPC achieved ∼ 52 % higher closed-loop performance than standalone RL and ∼ 80 % higher performance than MPC with the same horizon length.

title: Physiology-guided multi-objective machine learning for robust fructose prediction in Asian pear under interannual climate variability
abstract: Predicting Asian pear fructose concentration under interannual climate variability is challenging because sugar accumulation reflects cumulative interactions among developmental progression, environmental conditions, and prior metabolic state. Using a six-year repeated-measures field dataset from ‘Niitaka’ Asian pear trees, fructose concentration at N days after full bloom (DAFB) was predicted from meteorological and phenological descriptors aligned to each DAFB sampling window and sugar measurements from the preceding sampling point (N − 15 DAFB). We developed a physiology-guided machine learning framework using XGBoost as a fixed regressor and three feature-transformation components: a climate gate that weights precursor-history signals by stage-specific environmental conditions, a Richards growth kernel that constrains developmental trajectories, and lagged sugar features that represent metabolic continuity. Representation parameters were optimized under six-fold leave-one-year-out cross-validation using scalarized single-objective optimization or nondominated sorting genetic algorithm III (NSGA-III), targeting the mean, maximum, and standard deviation of yearwise root mean square error (RMSE). The selected multi-objective model achieved a pooled RMSE of 35.48 mg·g −1 dry weight (DW), compared with 55.53 mg·g −1 DW for the climate–phenology baseline, reducing pooled error by 36.1% and interannual variability by 70.4%. Pareto front analysis revealed an accuracy–robustness trade-off and supported the selection of an operationally balanced solution for reliable fruit-quality prediction.

title: Hyperspectral olive maturity estimation model for table olives: A non-invasive proof-of-concept study
abstract: The economic significance of olive cultivation and trade is paramount for Mediterranean countries, yielding a substantial impact on their respective local economies. However, the quality of olives is significantly influenced by the harvest timing, which occurs when they reach optimal size and maturity stage. Conventionally, farmers have relied on empirical observation to determine the optimal harvest date, guided by their accumulated expertise and knowledge. While this approach is well-founded, it lacks the rigor and objectivity offered by data-driven methods. The development of an automatic system for determining olive maturity is a significant concern for the industry. This study proposes an artificial intelligence-based system for estimating the maturity of table olives using a novel technological approach. The method involves the identification of olive maturity stages through field methods that utilize proximal hyperspectral imaging technology. A comprehensive analysis was conducted to elucidate the importance of each spectral band and to assess the model’s performance with a reduced feature space. In this proof-of-concept study, a Hyperspectral Olive Maturity Estimation Model (HOMEM) was developed to estimate olives’ maturity by determining their Maturity Index. The model employed visible and near-infrared spectral signatures acquired through in-field hyperspectral imaging. The present study explores the precision of HOMEM and the impact of normalization with hyperspectral images employing various AI-based models. The proposed HOMEM model attained an R2 value of 93 % in its estimation of the Maturity Index through the utilization of visible and near-infrared wavelengths. The results of this study demonstrate the potential of hyperspectral imaging and machine learning techniques to enhance the assessment of olive quality and reduce reliance on traditional, experience-based methods.

title: Structure over sound: A free box count out-predicts in-hive acoustics for honey-bee colony strength
abstract: In-hive microphones are widely promoted for non-invasive estimation of honey-bee colony strength (frames of bees), and benchmarks report near-perfect accuracy. Whether that accuracy survives on unseen colonies and apiaries decides deployability. We re-analysed two open multi-sensor datasets, UrBAN (ten urban colonies) and MSPB (53 rural colonies at two apiaries), harmonised to a shared 20-feature acoustic space with in-hive temperature and humidity. Random forests and hierarchical mixed models were evaluated under progressively stricter validation, from random k -fold to leave-one-apiary-out and cross-dataset transfer, with the acoustic, environmental and structural contributions separated by ablation. Most of the reported skill is not acoustic. Under leave-one-apiary-out validation the acoustic features alone reach R 2 = 0.17 , in-hive temperature and humidity alone 0.56, and the beekeeper’s box count alone 0.71; the box count from the previous visit, fixed before the label existed, still reaches 0.42 alone and 0.55 with climate. Adding acoustics never improved accuracy materially under any configuration tested ( Δ R 2 between −0.12 and ＋0.02). The box count’s 90% conformal intervals keep near-nominal empirical coverage across apiaries, while those of the sensor model cover 70% of cases in one transfer direction and 99% in the other. In an exploratory cross-dataset comparison, limited by a 17-assessment audio-matched UrBAN sample, the box count transferred in both directions and the acoustic features in neither. A plausible reason is sensing geometry: the microphone sits in the bottom brood box, which barely varies, while almost all population variation is above it. The box count mixes physical capacity with management decisions. It is therefore a diagnostic baseline and not a measurement instrument, and the finding is that a single bottom-box microphone adds nothing to it, though acoustics retain value for other targets. The conclusion rests on the within-MSPB cross-apiary comparison and is limited to a single bottom-box microphone, the shared feature space and the frames-of-bees target.

title: Dynamic real-time detection of maize ear dehusking clearance rate based on deep learning and multi-object tracking
abstract: Real-time assessment of maize-ear dehusking clearance rate is important for monitoring harvesting quality, but dynamic harvesting conditions can cause missed detections, false positives, and duplicate counting due to background interference, target-scale variation, motion blur, and severe occlusion. This study presents a real-time dehusking-clearance-rate monitoring framework integrating object detection, multi-object tracking, and identity-based duplicate-aware counting. An improved You Only Look Once version 11 nano (YOLOv11n) detector, termed PPSE-YOLO, was constructed by incorporating a Partial Frequency Dynamic Convolution-based C3k2 module (PFD_C3k2), the Pyramid Sparse Transformer (PST), and a Separated and Enhancement Attention Module (SEAMHead). PFD_C3k2 improves frequency- and texture-related feature representation under background interference and motion blur, PST enhances selective multi-scale feature fusion for maize ears with different apparent sizes, and SEAMHead strengthens the representation of visible features under partial occlusion. BoT-SORT maintains target identities across consecutive frames, and the resulting trajectories are converted into unique counting events for continuous dehusking-clearance-rate estimation. PPSE-YOLO achieved a Precision of 92.7%, a Recall of 91.8%, and an mAP@0.5 of 95.5%, representing improvements of 2.4, 0.9, and 1.5 percentage points, respectively, over YOLOv11n. Meanwhile, its computational complexity and parameter count were reduced from 6.3 to 5.1 GFLOPs and from 2.58 to 2.28 M, respectively. BoT-SORT achieved an MOTA of 92.05% and an IDF1 of 89.87%. At the system level, the framework achieved an overall counting consistency of 97.67%, a mean absolute dehusking-clearance-rate estimation error of 2.02 percentage points across 10 test groups, and an average end-to-end processing speed of 34 FPS. These results indicate the feasibility of the framework for real-time maize dehusking monitoring under the tested harvesting conditions.

title: Forecasting drought across Canada using a hybrid machine learning approach: a national perspective for adaptations and early warning systems
abstract: Drought is a major natural hazard in Canada, with significant socio-economic impacts across the country’s diverse climatic and geographic regions. This study proposes a hybrid forecasting framework that combines fast adaptive empirical mode decomposition (FAEMD), an ensemble deep random vector functional link (edRVFL) network, and the energy valley optimizer (EVO) to model nonstationary hydrological time series. Using 74 years (1951–2024) of meteorological data from 24 Canadian meteorological stations, we first identified substantial spatial variability and nonstationary trends in historical drought conditions. The proposed FAEMD-edRVFL-EVO framework was then used to forecast the Standardized Precipitation Evapotranspiration Index (SPEI 12 ) at one-, two-, and three-month lead times and compared against standalone and hybrid implementations of extreme gradient boosting, random forest, and k -nearest neighbor algorithms. FAEMD-edRVFL-EVO consistently achieved the best performance, with median correlation coefficients of 0.999, 0.980, and 0.906 for one-, two-, and three-month forecasts, respectively. Performance remained strong in climatically complex regions, particularly in Western and Northern Canada. By effectively isolating nonstationary signals, this applied study demonstrates that the integrated pipeline provides a scalable, accurate, and computationally efficient practical solution for large-scale drought forecasting and early warning under increasing climatic uncertainty.

title: Estimating and Forecasting Grapevine Phenology using Deep Learning and Mechanistic models: A comparative study
abstract: Accurate monitoring of key phenological stages, such as bud-break, blooming, veraison, and berries ripe, is essential for optimizing vineyard management, especially in the context of climate change. Grapevine phenology, primarily driven by temperature, has been extensively studied with the most common prediction methods based on the growing-degree-days (GDD) approach. In this paper we propose and compare two novel methodologies, respectively based on a mechanistic and a deep learning approach, to detect and forecast key phenological stages. The mechanistic model simulates the effects of both air temperature and water availability on the major plant metabolic processes that drive the annual phenological cycle (vegetative and reproductive growth, and sugar accumulation in the berry), whereas the deep learning model, based on a Recurrent Neural Network, infers directly the phenological cycle taking as input the time series of the daily weather station measurements. Using seven years of phenological data collected from five grape varieties (‘Aglianico’, ‘Greco’ ‘Syrah’, ‘Touriga Franca’, and ‘Touriga Nacional’) across four Mediterranean sites in Italy, Spain, and Portugal, we evaluate the performance of these models against traditional GDD-based methods. Cross-validation results show that while the mechanistic model excels at predicting bud-break, with a Mean Absolute Error (MAE) of 4.9 days compared to 5.7 and 5.6 days of the GDD-based and the deep learning model, respectively, the deep learning model is an all-around optimal methodology in terms of predicting accuracy across different stages, resulting in an overall MAE slightly under 5 days, with an average error reduction of 0.6 to 1.6 days respect to the two GDD-based models tested. Furthermore, we illustrate how these models can leverage sub-seasonal weather forecasts to predict phenological events in advance, offering practical tools for vineyard managers. This was particularly true for the deep learning model, that was able to predict grapevine phenological stages two weeks in advance with an average error lower than 6 days. These findings highlight the potential of these novel approaches for automating phenology monitoring and improving decision-making in viticulture under changing climate conditions.
